name: Bilal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead an excavator crew at a large mine. I check the wall, service book and haul route before anyone starts a cut. My two-year technical diploma and long practice make me the person the crew calls when the ground moves. I use AI daily to sort fault notes, but the lower rate here and thin savings have made money a separate worry.

say: I think **checklists** may save minutes if the lead still verifies the machine.
I use **AI fault notes** daily, but I check the manual before directing the crew.
think: I welcome **limited AI change**, yet our household budget is already tight.
I have **three weeks** saved despite being a team lead.
do: **Lead** excavator shifts and check automated lists against the fault book.
**Transfer** one percent of each full pay packet to savings if regular bills fit.
feel: **Anxious** about low pay and thin savings, with little fear of mild AI.
S0.quote: My excavator lead title does not add weeks to our savings account.
fieldNote: **Lead standing** coexists with lower pay and a three-week cushion after family help.
**Daily AI use** is established practice; this scenario does not add a new learning action.

steps.text: Keep leading excavator shifts and checking the fault book
Transfer one percent of full pay packets if regular bills fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a better checklist might save me ten minutes, but the excavator still needs someone who knows the wall. I use an AI tool every day to sort fault notes, then check the manual and the machine before I give an instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like a quiet AI year, but our finances are not quiet. My lead title comes with a low rate at this mine, and we have only three weeks of costs saved after helping a grown child move. A lost shift would go straight into the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading excavator shifts and compare any automated checklist with the actual fault book. In the first year I would move a small fixed amount from each full pay packet into savings before considering another family expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money, even if the technology barely moves. My excavator lead title does not add weeks to our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the fixed amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with one percent of a full pay packet, and stop if the regular bills do not fit. I would show my partner the balance at each month end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the checklist tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test it on a familiar hydraulic fault and ask the mechanic to check the output. If it gets the wrong excavator model, I would not put it on the crew’s shift sheet.

say: I expect **office scheduling** to change before excavator operation.
I would test **dispatch routes** against actual blocked ramps.
think: I think **physical shifts** will continue near term, with robot cuts possible later.
I could not absorb **even small cuts** with three weeks saved and few local mines.
do: **Test** approved dispatch routes against blocked ramps on paid time if offered.
**Log** route errors with time, marker and closure reason.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, while interested in a useful trial.
S1.quote: A clever route is useless when the ramp is shut.
fieldNote: **Field testing** matches his adaptive style, with dated route evidence rather than a sales claim.
**Office colleague** is a named person whose work he expects to change first.
**Thin cushion** keeps him anxious even while his own physical shifts look safe near term.

steps.text: Test approved dispatch routes on paid time if a trial is offered
Log closed-ramp errors with time and road marker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew planning software can help place trucks, but an excavator operator still has to read the wall. I would test a new dispatch display with our real blocked routes before anyone calls it ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office schedulers could lose tasks first. My excavator work is physical, so I expect my shifts to continue near term, but slower robots might trim the crew later. With three weeks saved and few nearby mines, even a small cut would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the shift lead above me for access to a new dispatch display once it is approved. In the first year I would run a paid comparison of screen routes against our actual blocked ramps if the mine offers a trial, and log errors for maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our small cushion, though I would enjoy making the tool more useful. A clever route is useless when the ramp is shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write the time, road marker and reason for each closure. A supervisor can test those details; a vague complaint will disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which scheduler comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coworker Nora builds the truck order and calls us when the weather changes. I would ask what parts of that job the software removes before cheering for a faster schedule.

say: I separate **2028 dispatch** change from excavator robots around 2031.
I want a **paid monitoring path** before experienced operators lose wall shifts.
think: I expect **sharp shift cuts** if capable robots handle the wall, even for a lead.
I cannot replace lost wages with **three weeks** saved and few nearby jobs.
do: **Check** monitoring-course requirements with the training office now.
**Take** the course after 2028 if a funded place and full pay are offered.
**Apply** for an advertised monitoring shift, or local plant work if none opens.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major roster cuts and sleepless money calculations.
S2.quote: I cannot trade a present wage for a promise about a future screen.
fieldNote: **High standing** does not shield him from expected cuts to excavator shift numbers.
**Funding and pay** must be confirmed before he enrols.
**Local plant work** is a fallback to a missing monitoring vacancy, not a guaranteed job.

steps.text: Take the monitoring course if funded and full pay continues
Apply for an advertised monitoring shift if one opens
Apply for local plant work if no monitoring post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI changes dispatch by 2028, but capable excavator robots arrive around 2031. We need a paid path into monitoring work before the mine removes experienced operators from the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots reach the excavator. I expect the mine to reduce the number of excavator shifts sharply if those machines handle the wall, including mine despite my lead title. With three weeks saved and few local mines, our income would drop faster than I could replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the mine training office for its monitoring-course requirements and tell my partner the possible dates. In the first year after 2028 I would take the course if the mine funds a place and keeps my pay, then apply for an advertised monitoring shift; if no post opens, I would apply for local plant jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wake in the night thinking about how many weeks we could live on the account if my roster were halved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the fees, paid hours and actual job notice before signing up. I cannot trade a present wage for a promise about a future screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown child help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my child what is changing, but I would not ask for money back from the move. My partner and I need a plan that works on our own pay.

say: I see **2031 dispatch** change before capable excavator robots around 2034.
I want **paid course rules** before workers give up wall shifts.
think: I may be **66** when robots arrive and still need wages.
I cannot treat **three weeks** saved as a retirement fund.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and monitoring-course pay rules.
**Enrol** after 2031 if a paid course place exists.
**Save** extra-shift pay after monthly essentials are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about wages and retirement income, with more time to check options.
S3.quote: I like trying new tools, but my partner cannot eat curiosity.
fieldNote: **Age 66** does not settle retirement with a three-week cushion and unverified pension.
**Paid place** is a condition for course enrolment, not a known benefit.
**Extra savings** depend on actual overtime and covered essentials.

steps.text: Enrol in monitoring training if a paid place exists
Save extra-shift pay if monthly essentials are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch changes in 2031 and capable excavator robots around 2034. The longer lead lets us test a monitoring course while we still have paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 by the robot date. I might be ready to reduce hours, but three weeks saved is no retirement plan, and I have not checked the pension against our bills. If the mine cuts wall shifts, I would still need wages somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a pension estimate this year and ask the mine to post the monitoring course pay rules. In the first year after 2031 I would enrol if the course is paid and a place exists, then save the pay from any extra shift after monthly essentials are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as rushed as the 2028 picture. Time helps only if the course and pension numbers turn into something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would calculate the difference beside rent and food before accepting. I like trying new tools, but my partner cannot eat curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a pension check reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare the monthly amount with our bills and ask an adviser if the figures confuse us. I will not leave the mine on a birthday alone.

say: I separate **2036 dispatch** change from excavator robots around 2039.
I want **training and pension** figures shared well before shifts change.
think: I hope to leave **full shifts** before robots arrive at 71.
I may still need **paid work** if pension income is too small.
do: **Keep** lead excavator shifts and familiar approved fault tools.
**Seek** pension advice with my partner after 2036.
**Apply** for local part-time yard work if the pension leaves a gap.
feel: **Anxious** about later income despite secure near-term shifts.
S4.quote: My next few shifts feel secure; my later income is the question.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots shifts attention to pension adequacy.
**Daily tool use** continues as normal and does not count as new learning here.
**Part-time stores work** is a possible local application, contingent on a pension gap.

steps.text: Keep lead excavator shifts and approved fault tools
Seek pension advice with my partner after 2036
Apply for local part-time yard work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches dispatch in 2036 and capable excavator robots around 2039. A decade is enough for the mine to train people and for families to check pension figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036 and 71 at the robot date. I hope to be off full shifts by then, but the thin account now makes me careful about that promise. If the pension falls short, I might still need a paid monitoring or yard role before a robot changes the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my lead shifts and use the approved fault tools I already know. In the first year after 2036 I would seek pension advice with my partner, then apply for a local part-time yard role if the pension leaves a monthly gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, though I can use the decade to prepare. My next few shifts feel secure; my later income is the question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What yard work would you seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our mine stores about a part-time equipment-check post, because I know the machines and the bus reaches the gate. I would read the pay notice before changing shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family to cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk with our grown children, but their incomes are not in my budget. I would rather work a few paid hours than hand them our bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable excavator robots around 2031 could sharply reduce my shifts at 63. A funded monitoring course with full pay and an advertised post would help me move before the roster is cut. I need the mine to publish the real numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the lead title pays when there is no shift to lead. A title will not cover rent if the excavator roster is halved.

headlineQuote: A title will not cover rent if the excavator roster is halved.
portrait: **Bilal, 58**, leads an excavator crew and uses AI daily for fault notes while checking every machine instruction.
**Lower pay** and only three weeks saved leave his household exposed despite high skill and a lead title.
**Early testing** appeals to him, especially paid dispatch trials with route errors recorded precisely.
**Fast AGI** alarms him because dispatch changes in 2028 and capable excavator robots could cut shifts sharply around 2031.
**Longer warning** gives him time to seek paid monitoring training and check pension income, which remains uncertain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected major excavator shift cuts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded monitoring training** with full pay and a real vacancy would give him a route to keep earning.
**Published roster numbers** would let his family plan before cuts arrive.
